title: Ergun Çağatay, bridge to the vast Turkic world
gist: Caroline Eden profiles Izmir-born photojournalist Ergun Çağatay, who after surviving the 1983 Orly Airport bombing spent years after the Soviet collapse photographing the Turkic-speaking world from Yakutia to Lithuania. His work shows shared linguistic, culinary and herding threads alongside sharp religious diversity, and his Moynaq trawler image captures the inherited Aral Sea disaster.

themes.theme: Origins of the Turkic photography project

insights.claim: Ergun Çağatay was badly burned in the 15 July 1983 bombing at the Turkish Airlines counter at Paris Orly Airport, which killed eight people, and could not resume photography for five years; during recovery he conceived a plan to photograph the entire Turkic-speaking world.
insights.speaker: Caroline Eden
insights.so_what: Background on the origin of a landmark visual record of Turkic peoples.

insights.claim: Çağatay's Turkic project only became feasible after the fall of the Soviet Union opened access to Turkic communities from eastern Siberia to Central Asia.
insights.speaker: Caroline Eden
insights.so_what: The post-Soviet opening of Central Asia created new cultural and economic links across the Turkic world.
insights.locator: It took not only this unforeseen disaster

insights.claim: Çağatay saw a gap: much was written about Turkic nomads' migration toward the Mediterranean, the Ottoman Empire and modern Turkey, but few looked at the wider Turkic world, and few people understood what 'Turkic' meant.
insights.speaker: Caroline Eden
insights.so_what: Pan-Turkic identity remains under-understood in the West despite its geopolitical relevance.
insights.quote: Few people, he said, really understood what ‘Turkic’ meant.
insights.locator: He had identified a gap in the market

themes.theme: Shared threads across the Turkic world

insights.claim: Turkic languages share cognates across thousands of miles: 'snow' is haar in Yakut, kar in Turkish, gar in Turkmen, qar in Uyghur and qor in Uzbek.
insights.speaker: Caroline Eden
insights.so_what: Linguistic kinship underpins soft-power ties Turkey cultivates across Central Asia and Siberia.
insights.locator: Keeping the Yakutian tundra in mind

insights.claim: Yakut speakers in eastern Siberia share herding and dairy traditions, such as fermented mare's milk, with the steppe peoples of Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan hundreds of miles away.
insights.speaker: Caroline Eden
insights.so_what: Shared pastoral culture links dispersed Turkic communities.
insights.locator: Keeping the Yakutian tundra in mind

insights.claim: Food traditions trace shared heritage: Lithuanian Karaim kybyn pastry resembles the chebureki turnover of Crimean Tatars.
insights.speaker: Caroline Eden
insights.so_what: Cuisine as evidence of cultural continuity.
insights.quote: When it comes to tracing the shared heritage of the scattered Turkic people, the view from the kitchen is illuminating.

insights.claim: Turkic speakers are not exclusively Sunni Muslim: they include shamanistic Tuvans of the Altai, Orthodox Christian Gagauz in Moldova, and Lithuania's Karaim, who practise an archaic form of Judaism.
insights.speaker: Caroline Eden
insights.so_what: Pan-Turkic identity cuts across religion, complicating assumptions that Turkic equals Muslim.
insights.quote: Turkic speakers are not exclusively Sunni Muslim

insights.claim: Only a couple of hundred Karaim live in Lithuania today, descendants of Turkic tribes brought by Grand Duke Vytautas in the 14th century to guard castles, yet their culture remains prominent in Trakai.
insights.speaker: Caroline Eden
insights.so_what: Small minorities can retain outsized cultural footprints.
insights.locator: There are photographs, too, of the Karaim

insights.claim: Çağatay's image of an abandoned trawler with children at Moynaq, Uzbekistan — a former fishing port that once employed over 30,000 people — shows how the Aral Sea disaster, caused by Soviet-era cotton irrigation, has passed its ecological and economic fallout to the next generation.
insights.speaker: Caroline Eden
insights.so_what: A stark case study in long-tail environmental and economic damage from resource-intensive agricultural policy.
insights.quote: he captures how the catastrophe has been passed on to the next generation

insights.claim: Çağatay is poorly remembered outside Turkey despite his landmark book Turkic-Speaking Peoples, distilled from 35,000 photos to 300; he died in 2018 while planning to document Crimean Tatars, the Balkans and the persecuted Uyghurs of northwest China.
insights.speaker: Caroline Eden
insights.so_what: Gaps remain in documenting politically sensitive Turkic groups such as the Uyghurs.
insights.quote: Ergun Çağatay is not well remembered outside Turkey, which is a shame
